speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
I should like to address a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, notice of which I sent him yesterday. It relates to the devaluation of the pound as it affects Canadians who served 45781-50
in the imperial forces. The minister wrote me a note yesterday which reads as follows:
I take it from your note that you will ask a question tomorrow under orders of the day. Perhaps you will send me a copy of your question, and I shall try to give a clear-cut reply.
I sent the minister a copy of my question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: DEVALUATION OF POUND STERLING-IMPERIAL EX-SERVICEMEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice yesterday of his intention to ask this question today.
First of all I wish to express regret that earlier discussions of this matter have been misinterpreted across the country, and I should like to make this statement as clear as I possibly can. The question which the hon. member sent me reads as follows:
I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. It is in relation to the devaluation of the pound regarding those imperial veterans who reside in Canada, as there has been considerable misunderstanding about the effect of this regarding those who live in Canada.
Would the minister clarify it, as it is said that those who have resided in Canada for some time would not lose any money by the same? I sent him some letters on this subject, and he wrote me yesterday as follows:
"Dear Mr. Church:
I am sorry if the matter has been misunderstood.
I take it from your note that you will ask a question tomorrow under orders of the day. Perhaps you will send me a copy of your question, and I shall try to give a clear-cut reply.
Sincerely,
Milton Gregg."
In reply I would say that a supplementary award from the Canadian pension commission is accorded to those Canadians who were domiciled in Canada prior to enlistment and who served in the imperial forces, and have been awarded a disability pension from the British ministry of pensions. To these Canadians our pension commission make a supplementary award bringing their pension up to the rate which they would have received had they served with Canadian forces. I should like to make it clear that this is a very special group who, naturally, are not worried. I now come to others who are worried, and about whom all of us are much concerned. No action is contemplated for those without prewar domicile in Canada whose disability pension from British sources is not being augmented or supplemented by the Canadian pension commission. Likewise no action is being taken with respect to those in receipt of long-service pensions, as distinct from disability pensions, from the British armed

subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act by increasing the amount of refund payable to members of the force in respect to prior service in a provincial police force where they were retained in the force beyond the maximum period of service that may be counted for the purpose of computing a pension.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution will lead to the introduction of a bill to provide a new basis for making the refund to certain members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There are members of that force who formerly served in the provincial forces and who, when they were taken into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to the end of securing for them pension rights with respect to service they had performed for the provincial forces, were called upon to make contributions to the pension fund in respect of the terms they had served with the provincial forces.
Several of this same group of R.C.M.P. members during the war rendered some excess service, beyond their ordinary terms, for a variety of reasons,-usually because they could not be replaced under wartime conditions. Heretofore they have been entitled to refunds arrived at by taking into account the period of their excess service, on the one hand, as related to their provincial service, on the other. But until the present time the calculation has been made on the basis of the total amount of the contribution

to the R.C.M.P. pension fund by both themselves and the province concerned. The amendment will provide that in arriving at this amount there shall be taken into account only that period of service in which they themselves have individually made contributions to the pension fund. This will have the effect of almost doubling the amount of refunds they secure.	,

subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD
speechtext: How many men will it affect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD

subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD

I did not hear the answer as to the numbers affected. When the minister is answering that question perhaps he will direct his attention to one or two other matters which I might be allowed to bring up at this time.
In view of the fact that this change is being made-incidentally it has been asked for by various members of the force, and requested on previous occasions from this side of the house-may I ask the minister whether, when amendments are being made to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, he will give consideration to making further amendments which have been requested by the R.C.M.P. veterans association.
I am sure that anything that can be done or any changes which can be made in the mounted police act which will improve the morale of the force would receive the support of all hon. members. Anomalous conditions such as the one now before us certainly ought to be removed in order to ensure the maintenance of the highest possible morale.
While giving my support to this measure- and I am sure support will be general throughout the house-I would ask the minister a question which has to do with veterans of the mounted police. Has consideration been given to providing former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with hospitalization, medical treatment, and so on, that is enjoyed by members of the armed forces? This matter, which has been brought up before in this house, is deserving of consideration.
I live in Prince Albert, which has been one of the principal centres of mounted police activity for years. In that city are a number of veterans who joined the force prior to 1900. Their numbers are not large. I am thinking particularly of two former members of the force who are now seventy-eight and eighty-two years of age respectively. These men find it impossible to live on the pension they receive. One of them served in the Riel rebellion of 1885, and the other joined in 1891. They feel that some assistance should be given to them.

These older veterans served in the force in the early days when the rate of pay was fifty cents a day. The minister will remember that increases in pay have been of comparatively recent origin. I have in mind other veteran police officers, two of whom served in the rebellion of 1885, and who were paid fifty cents per day for many years. The pension they receive today is small, being based on the amount they were paid at the time they were discharged. These men feel that they are entitled to an increase in pension in order that their standard of living may be at least equal to that of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were discharged in recent years.
The mounted police today is a specialized, highly trained and efficient body, and anything we can do to raise its standards or to indicate our appreciation of its work should be done. I suggest that, in the interests of improving morale in the R.C.M.P., these older veterans should be given a greater opportunity to enjoy life than they have under the present regulations.

subtopic: INCREASE IN REFUND PAYABLE IN RESPECT TO PRIOR SERVICE BEYOND MAXIMUM PENSION PERIOD

I think we can

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, 1946, to increase the salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada and to provide salaries for an increased number of judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario; also to amend the present provision respecting travelling allowances to a judge of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think this resolution is explained by its own terms, but perhaps I should refer to the third part, which reads:
-also to amend the present provision respecting travelling allowances to a judge of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick.
Formerly there was only one judge in the city of Moncton, New Brunswick, but a recent provincial statute provides for two, and this is a consequential enactment to take care of that change.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think there are one or two comments which should be made on this proposal. I do not believe anyone should take it on himself to say at this stage that the resolution should not carry and that the legislation to be founded on it should not pass. But I think it is about time that we scrutinized more carefully these proposed increases in the salaries of judges. As an hon. member to my left has just remarked- I am sure he will not mind if I repeat his words-they are almost becoming an annual affair. No one is going to object to our judges being paid salaries commensurate with the dignity and responsibility of their positions. I know, as other hon. members do, that most top-ranking lawyers can earn more in private practice than they can on the bench, even with the increases in judges' salaries which have so far been granted. But it is important to bear in mind that by recent amendments to the Judges Act, judges are now entitled, and properly so, to generous retirement allowances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Noncontributory, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
These privileges do not pertain to private practice. No longer can it be said of judges that the emoluments of office are unattractive. It is my view that the time has come for us to serve notice that increases in judges' salaries will not be accepted in the future without the closest scrutiny.
There is a most important principle to be borne in mind. The administration of justice must be such as to have the confidence of the people of Canada. Our courts and our judges must have the confidence of the people. If we go on year after year increasing the salaries of our judges, the people of Canada are going to object. It will arouse in the minds of the people a feeling of resentment against the bench, because they will believe that all that judges have to do is to request increases in salary and they get them, while the average person has to work and struggle for his increases. I certainly believe that before we go further in increasing salaries in the top brackets we should see whether we cannot increase the salaries of men in the lower brackets who have families to support.
I repeat that the time has come when the tendency to grant increases in salaries to top government executives and to the judiciary must come to an end. We serve notice that, in the future, proposals for increases in salary will not be accepted without the closest scrutiny.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister inform the committee as to the amounts of the salary increases proposed in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is contrary to the rules of the house to disclose the contents of a bill at the committee stage. That is one reason why I made my explanatory remarks so brief. I thought we could discuss much more intelligently the justification for the increases if we had the amounts before us in the form of a bill. If we fall into the habit of attempting to discuss the contents of bills that are not before us at the resolution stage, it is a practice that can only lead to confusion, and will not really give us the best results for the time we spend in considering the legislation.
As to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops, I might direct his attention to the fact that this is a proposal to increase the salaries of the judges of the supreme court only. It arises out of the fact that, by the bill which was passed by the house a few days ago, we have greatly increased the responsibilities of that court. Since it is to be the court of last resort for Canada, we must take every necessary step to make sure that we obtain the services

of men of the highest ability for the membership of that court. As I say, I am quite prepared, when the bill is before the house on second reading and the amount of the increase is known, to justify the increase which the government seeks.
I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops will agree that, although he may have had some reservations as to the propriety of abolishing appeals to the privy council, once we create a court of last resort in Canada it is of the greatest importance that we secure as members of that court men of the highest talents. The membership of the supreme court is drawn from all parts of Canada. When we make an appointment to the court- I think this is true in all cases-we select a man who is a leader of the bar in his own province, who is of reasonably mature age, and who in most cases has family ties and a home in the province in which he lives. We ask him to pull up the roots which he has been spending a lifetime putting down, and to move his family and his home into an entirely new sphere. To such men in relation to what in most cases has been the very much larger income that he had been earning up until that time, we have to offer some fairly substantial financial inducement to bring him to the supreme court bench.
I am sure the hon. members for Kamloops and Vancouver East will also agree that any moneys we lay out in a wise provision of this sort, provided that we administer it properly, will pay substantial dividends to the Canadian nation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: I want to support the views that have been expressed by the hon. member for Kamloops, and by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East, but the main reason I rise at this moment is that frankly I was disturbed by the position the minister took when he went so far as to say that it was not proper to include in the resolution preceding the bill the amounts of money involved. On the contrary the minister is not maintaining the traditions of the house when he fails to put in those amounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I did not say that it was not proper to put the amounts in. I said it was not proper at the resolution stage of the bill to discuss the contents of the bill. Whether it was right or wrong not to include the amounts of the salaries in the resolution, the fact is that the resolution that is before us does not state the amounts of the salaries, and we shall not have that until the bill comes down. Under these circumstances I submit it is not proper to discuss that now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to protest strenuously against this practice being followed
Judges Act
so often, particularly during this session- and it happened a few times during the last session as well. I am glad to note that the Speaker is in the chamber, although I am not asking him to participate in the discussion, either on my side or against it. But he will remember quite well being in your place, Mr. Chairman, when this whole issue was fought out in respect to an old age pension bill back in 1947. As we were able to point out at that time, it had been the practice of the government down through the years, in a resolution preceding a bill which had the recommendation of the governor general, to indicate in the resolution the amount of money which would be involved if that bill passed. I refer to the incident of June 26, 1947, because on that occasion a minister introduced a resolution preceding a bill without stating the amount, and some of us were able to argue, from many precedents and citations in the books, that this gave the committee, when it dealt with the bill in the committee stage, the right to move amendments asking for higher amounts. I could demonstrate my point by saying that that is the position in which the minister finds himself now. I can assure him that when he brings in his bill with the increased salaries I shall not take advantage of the opportunity to move that the salaries be made higher still.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Then why is the hon. member raising the question? What is the purpose?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Because I want the Minister of Justice to follow the rules of this house. Citation 436 of Beauchesne reads:
The governor general's recommendation to any resolution involving a payment out of the public treasury must be formally given by a privy councillor in his place ... as soon as the motion has been proposed for the house to go into committee on the resolution.
Then citation 439:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making a certain expenditure. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and debate is confined to the resolution which should not be lengthy . . .
Note this:
. . . although care must be taken that the terms used are sufficiently wide to cover the whole of the bill which will be subsequently introduced.
Then citation 440:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the governor general's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended.
And citation 445:
It may happen that the resolution sanctions some expenditure without fixing the maximum amount to be spent. If, for instance, the resolution recom-

Judges Act
mends that adequate salaries be paid a newly constituted body and the amounts of the salaries are fixed in the bill based on that resolution, the committee on the bill has the right to increase those amounts, because, in doing so, it does not go beyond the scope of the royal recommendation.
From all these citations, and from the practice that has been followed by this house down through the years, as well as that followed in the United Kingdom, it is clear that the principle of governmental responsibility in respect to expenditures makes it necessary, or at least highly desirable, that when the government indicates the recommendation of the governor general it should indicate to the house to what extent that expenditure is to go.
As I have said already, I do not intend to take advantage of this opportunity to move that the amounts be increased; but I might draw to the attention of the minister citation 486, which applies particularly because of the way in which this resolution has been worded:
Reductions can be made in committee on the bill . . .
And later:
The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers have inserted in the bill; and, when no amount has been mentioned in the resolution-
That is the pitfall into which the minister has fallen here.
-any member may propose to increase the grants specified in the bill or to extend the application of the provisions of the bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
I ask the minister to take time to look back over our recent history. If he will look up the resolution which preceded the family allowance measure introduced in 1944, he will find that it contained full details as to the amount to be paid each child and the amount to be paid in respect of successive children in the family. If he will look at the resolution which preceded the old age pension measure and all the amendments thereto, except the one in June, 1947, when this whole issue came up, he will find that they contain all the details. I could go on and refer also to veterans legislation, housing bills, and so on. It has been the practice down through the years, and I submit that it is consistent with the whole concept of governmental responsibility in money matters for the government to indicate in the resolution preceding a money bill the total amount of money involved. If it is true, as the books say time and again, that only with the royal recommendation can money measures be laid before the house, that carries with it a responsibility to tell us, when the measure is laid before us, how much money is involved. Otherwise

we would have the government going to the governor general and seeking approval for a blank cheque, keeping the details a secret until a later stage, as the minister is doing today.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not doubt that the Minister of Labour knows.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: I bow to Solomon's wisdom.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: The minister may know, but it is being kept secret from the rest of us, and this is not consistent with the whole concept of responsible government. The Minister of Justice says it is not desirable to discuss details at the resolution stage, that we must abide by the rules. He is one of the past masters in this house at discussing the details of a bill on second reading. That is out of order, but often he gets away with it. I hope that from now on the Minister of Justice and other ministers will take greater care to do what Beauchesne says should be done, and have the resolutions preceding the bill make clear what is involved in the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the committee owes me a vote of thanks for having provided the occasion for a fine statement on the rules of the house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I am sure we were all greatly edified by it; I know I was. I would point out to the hon. member, however, that within a very short time the bill will be brought down. If at that time there are in the house enough hon. members opposed to the amount of money involved, I presume the bill will be defeated and the purpose discussed by my hon. friend will be served. But having heard the statement of the hon. gentleman I think we might very well get on with the business and bring in the bill. Then we can see whether or not the amounts mentioned are excessive.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The situation that has
developed today is becoming a regular practice in the house. We had it a few evenings ago in connection with the overseas telecommunications resolution. The minister in charge on that occasion either did not have or would not give the information required. We had it yesterday on the fisheries bill, and today we have it on this resolution. I should like someone on the government side to tell us the purpose of bringing a resolution before this house and this committee if we are not to be given any information as to the purpose it is to fulfil. How are we to know whether or not we are in favour of this resolution- because the resolution has to be voted upon-

if we do not know what it contains? I quite agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said. What was placed before the governor general? What did he agree to? Surely this house is making a farce of parliamentary procedure by acting in this way. I warn this government that in the country today many people are greatly disturbed because of the composition of this house, with the top-heavy government majority. Further, I would warn the government not to use that majority for the purpose of departing from the accepted procedure in dealing with matters of this kind.
I want to oppose the resolution, and the bill, no matter what is in it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext: No matter what amount of money is in it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.

speechtext:
Would it be permissible, Mr. Chairman, to ask a general question even though section 1 has been passed? I have brought up this matter on previous occasions. I refer to the continuance of the anomalous requirement that a fiat of the crown is necessary before an action can be commenced against the crown.
I read what the minister said in this regard some days ago. He did not deny that it was
TMr. Garson.]
an anomalous state of affairs that a fiat should be required, but undertook to answer it by way of evasion and avoidance, as I read his argument. He said fiats were never refused. Well, if that were correct the obvious question would be, then why continue a formula that has no efficacy under modern practice? Today the crown is engaged in business, yet a fiat is required before an action can be commenced, as far as emanations of the crown are concerned. In the United Kingdom this state of affairs was done away with as of January 1, 1948. The doctrine that the king can do no wrong was admitted to be no longer applicable in so far as actions against the crown are concerned. This fiction of the law, no longer having any application to the complexities of modern conditions, was abrogated.
I should like to challenge the statement of the minister that a fiat is never refused. Fiats are refused, and have been refused in this country in the last thirteen or fourteen years under this government. I shall be specific in my statements. I have reference to the administration of the Indian department. Conditions existing on many of the reserves of this country require to be rectified, yet Indians residing on reserves find it impossible to commence an action against the crown, however justifiable that action might be, owing to the refusal of the crown to issue fiats. I recall one very good case. Some of the Indians on one of the reserves in Saskatchewan commenced an action against the Department of the Interior. In that action, which was heard by the late Mr. Justice MacLean, substantial damages were awarded -speaking from recollection I believe they ran to $25,000 or $30,000-for malfeasance or certainly nonfeasance on the part of officials of the department. Following that, Indians on another reserve requested the right to take action with respect to matters concerning them, but a fiat was refused.
An action by Indians is one case in which a fiat should not be refused. The Indian operates under a handicap by reason of the fact that he is subject to control by and a ward of the state; and whenever Indians feel there is an injustice, they should have a right of action against the crown. I ask the minister the reason for continuing this anomaly of requiring a fiat from the crown when a subject of His Majesty feels that he has been aggrieved. I hold no brief directly or indirectly for the Indians, nor did I act in the case to which I referred. It assures all those cases coming under the supervision of the Department of Justice and makes certain that the same principles of law are applied to all claims against the crown. In a great many cases our investigation, which is made by our officers, is of some service to the claimant. If settlement can be obtained without any legal action at all, that is certainly true.

I believe that we should be grateful and not dig up what the minister said here at one time and there at another time: "how many bushels of barley it takes to feed a pig", "how many cents that

barley costs", and other trivial items of that kind, in an effort to impede the business of the house and to try to place the minister in an embarrassing position over some quibbling little point. If we do not interrupt the business of government too much I think we will get something done, but this afternoon was a pretty sad exhibition of conducting the business of government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to clear up a point raised a few moments ago. I have in my hand yesterday's Hansard, and in the last paragraph, at the bottom righthand corner of page 768, I find the following words:
Therefore somebody ought to do something about establishing the capital works. We said that we were prepared to put in the main dam.
I do not know how I could have made it any clearer than that. It goes on:
In other words we were prepared to establish the storage in the St. Mary's river and thus start to utilize waters which otherwise might have been taken into the United States.
That is just as clear as I made it a few moments ago, that we are prepared to build the dam on this project. There was never any question about that. After the words I have quoted we began to discuss the question of how we are going to share the cost below the dam.

Yesterday and today emphasis has been placed on dams in their larger aspects and on large-scale methods of irrigation in the west. I think the success of any particular venture in connection with the operation of P.F.R.A., the operation of government, the operation of social services or anything else, must be judged on balance so that we have a true perspective of the whole picture and will not give consideration only to one thing thereby encouraging it and developing it to the detriment of something else. Valuable and necessary as these larger projects are, we should not adopt the attitude in connection with P.F.R.A. that they are the only ones that will happen in the future. I think no one is qualified to speak on P.F.R.A. unless he has had in his hands and has studied the thirteenth annual report of the P.F.R.A. administration with the record of achievement of P.F.R.A. over a seven-year period. If you study that document you will reach a balance in regard to what P.F.R.A. is trying to do not only on a large scale, but also, and what is perhaps more necessary, in a smaller way during the interval of time necessary to maintain certain people in drought areas of western Canada until these larger projects are in operation so that they may avail themselves of them. To give an idea of what is happening under P.F.R.A. let me read the introduction to the thirteenth annual report.

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, but you are to be forgiven for being confused. Item 30 was the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Item 32 is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We are now on item 31, major irrigation and water conservation projects in the prairie provinces.

In the first place I think it is only coming to the minister that he should be highly commended for the work he has done through P.F.R.A. I believe everyone recognizes that the work the minister has done in water conservation in western Canada is commendable in the highest degree. I doubt very much that any other Canadian statesman has made anything like as great a record in preserving the natural resources of Canada and developing the country. I think the minister is entitled to those words of praise and I do not believe they are overstatements in any sense of the word.
I should like to say a word or two on the general situation confronting the country in respect to the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project. May I say that I recognize there is no man in the Dominion of Canada who has the interests of the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project more at heart than the Minister of Agriculture. For that he is also to be highly commended.
I think a word or two will be in order for the sake of new members of the house so as to bring them up to date about the development of that most important project.
On February 17, 1941, there was appointed by order in council a committee called the Meek committee. It consisted of three members. The first was Victor Meek, who was controller of the dominion water and power bureau at Ottawa. He was the selection of the Minister of Mines and Resources. Then there was George Spence, director of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act activities. He was the selection of the Minister of Agriculture. Both of those men were excellent selections. Then there was William E. Hunter, of the accounts branch, Ottawa, the selection of the Minister of Finance. I presume Mr. Hunter possesses just as fine qualities as the other two gentlemen, but I do not have personal acquaintance with him on which to base a judgment. These men were chosen to examine into the St. Mary and Milk rivers water development and to make a report. Their

Supply-Agriculture
report was issued in February, 1942. Hon. members who have just entered the house will be interested to know that they can obtain it in the House of Commons by approaching the right man who has charge of reports and papers. If they want to study the whole question they will find plenty of reading matter and entertainment for several days.
The report is an excellent one, scientific, objective, exhaustive and full of good things from cover to cover. I think the Meek committee deserve the highest commendation for the work they did.
The Meek committee said a number of things which have an important bearing on the situation before us at the present time. In the first place they said that an agreement should be worked out and signed by the federal government and the provincial government before work begins. I fear such an agreement has not been worked out and signed even up to the present time. Who is to blame? I do not know. Probably it is just "one of those things", and nobody is to blame, but the simple fact that stares us in the face is that the agreement apparently has not been worked out and has not been signed.
The result is that neither side knows enough to say exactly enough where it is going, to be happy about the situation. We have to take that as a part of the circumstances surrounding the matter. I should like to read certain words which form the basis of the statement I have made, and which are to be found at page 8 of the report. They are:
The construction of the main reservoirs and connecting canals would provide the necessary facilities to store in Canada Canada's share of these international waters and would thereby be an insurance against the loss of a valuable resource.
Here I interject a few words for the benefit of those who are new members of this parliament. These are international waters. Consequently, according to international usage, they should be divided between Canada and the United States. Meetings were held in 1909, 1915 and 1921, as a result of which there was a division which was highly satisfactory to Canada.
It is understood among nations that when a country has a share of international waters and does not make beneficial use of its share, the other nation with a claim to those waters is perfectly in order in moving to reopen the question and in asking for a reallocation. That is the position that has confronted Canada. Unfortunately we did not make the progress after 1921 that we should have made in providing for the beneficial use of our share of the waters. It is better not to lay the blame on anyone, but the fact is that we did not do it. As a
result, by 1935 the situation had become serious; by 1940 it had become very serious, and now it is even worse. Thus we can realize the meaning of the passage I just read. Now I go on to the next sentence:
The construction of the main reservoirs and connecting canals is, however, not enough and unless provision is made, by extension of irrigation works to provide for beneficial and productive use, the expenditure involved by the dominion would not of course be justified.
Then I read the next paragraph, which is also relevant to the present debate:
For this reason the committee considers that before any construction is undertaken there should be an agreement between the province and the dominion that the province will undertake to construct the remaining irrigation works required to put the water to beneficial use and assume responsibility for maintenance and operation of all works. This agreement, we believe, should be conclusive and should set out, without any ground for doubt or misinterpretation, a distinct division as between provincial and dominion responsibility. It should be ratified by legislative action.
If I may interject a word again, unfortunately that wise suggestion has not been complied with. That is partly why we had a little unhappiness in this chamber last evening. We should not permit ourselves to feel so strongly toward each other however that we cannot get on with the job. Somehow or other we must devise ways and means of making up for the oversight which has occurred, remembering that the war intervened and that following the war there were reconstruction problems which commanded the attention of men both in Edmonton and in Ottawa.
Now I go on with the next paragraph:
The committee therefore suggests as a first step, that such an agreement be entered into between the dominion and the province. This agreement should provide for a co-operative development of the proposed project as broadly outlined in the foregoing paragraph.
That is all I desire to read from that section of the report. Hon. members will realize that we have really fallen into some difficulty because we have not heeded the counsel of this group of wise men. Now I am going forward with the next paragraph of their report:
The committee further suggests that a reasonable basis for division of costs may be as follows-
Before I proceed with that may I comment on the fact that the minister just now read his statement from yesterday's Hansard, in which he set forth that the dominion agreed to build the main dam. Well, when the estimates were first drawn up the main dam would account for an expenditure of about $4 million out of an estimated total of $13 million for the whole project. It is a fine thing for the dominion to agree to build that dam, and all credit is due them; but it must
[Mr. Blackmore.l

be borne in mind that the cost of the project including the dam, the canals, the distributing ditches, the reservoirs and so on is very substantial. The minister indicated complete willingness on the part of the dominion to share the cost of those subsidiary canals and reservoirs. Right there, in connection with the division of those costs, as to where the line of demarcation shall be drawn, is the point at which disagreement will arise. We must face this situation like the statesmen I am sure the members of this house intend to be and are, and like the statesmen I am sure the members of the Alberta house intend to be and are. We must iron out whatever difficulties there may be, make the very best of it and get on with the job. The committee suggested that the dominion should construct, as a one hundred per cent responsibility, the necessary facilities to store Canada's share of these international waters. We must give careful thought to the actual meaning of that expression. If we do so we see that a great deal of responsibility is placed by the committee upon the dominion government. These facilities to store the water should include all the reservoirs, of which there are at least seven, and the canals connecting those reservoirs so the water may be stored in them and the total quantity of water belonging to Canada preserved. That would be one interpretation. There may be others, but that is what the committee said. Now I read the committee's own words from the bottom of page 8:
That the dominion undertake and assume as a one hundred per cent responsibility the construction of the main reservoirs-
Notice that the word is in the plural.
*-and connecting canals to provide storage facilities for Canada's share of the waters of the St. Mary and Milk rivers as apportioned under the order of the international joint commission of October 4, 1921.
There is a considerable amount of accuracy and definiteness in that expression, perhaps not enough but it was the best they could do. Those words formed a good basis for the agreement. Then the committee went on to suggest that the province of Alberta construct and carry out as a one hundred per cent responsibility the balance of the program outlined in section 9 of part 2 of this report. Section 9 contains sufficient reading for about five days, and I shall not endeavour to even give a synopsis of it, but that is what the committee said. Now I read their own words from page 9:
That the province of Alberta construct and carry out as a one hundred per cent provincial responsibility, the balance of the proposed construction program as outlined in section 9 of part 2 of this report, or such changes of this program as may be found necessary and agreed to by the provincial and dominion governments.

I believe all hon. members will agree that statement is fairly specific.
Still reading from page 9, I quote:
That the province of Alberta be wholly responsible for maintenance and operation as well as replacements after the construction of main reservoirsnotice the word "reservoirs" is in the plural again.
-and connecting canals-
"canals" in the plural.
-has been completed by the dominion.
Again that is fairly specific, is it not? That would constitute the basis upon which both the province and dominion would proceed and naturally the thinking of both governments will be coloured by that background. If there is disagreement between the two, let us recognize that it is an honest disagreement. Each side believes it is right and there are no ulterior motives or delinquency on the part of either group.
There is a further recommendation that the amount of administration and the amount payable by the farmer, as well as the rate of repayment by the farmer, shall all be under provincial jurisdiction. I have not read the remarks the minister made last night, but I thought I gathered from what he said that he felt a little less happy because the province would have the handling of that.
No, I am not. As a matter of fact, my position is that they ought to do it and that they ought to pay their share.

I do not want to say very much about it because I have not read the minister's words, but here are the words used by the commission. It was stipulated that there should be an agreement between the two governing bodies on the matter of ultimate settlement and colonization. As everyone who has had anything to do with an irrigation project knows, that is a major consideration. After the project is completed, provision must be made to make sure there are good people on the project who are able to make a living.
May I read from the report in this connection? I read from page 9:
That the province of Alberta have full jurisdiction with respect to arrangements it may make with its municipalities, irrigation districts or others, as regards repayment of capital or for service charges necessary to the maintenance, operation and replacement of works.
That the suggested agreement should provide, among other things, for ultimate settlement and colonization.
Now, that is what the two governments started with and, really, they have not got beyond that yet. Perhaps the members of

the committee would be interested in knowing something about the reservoirs which are involved. On page 181 of the Meek report, there is a list of reservoirs involved in building the whole project. First, there is the St. Mary reservoir capable of storing 270,000 acre-feet of water. Then, there is the Chin reservoir enlargement capable of storing 150,000 acre-feet; the Verdigris reservoir, 140,500 acre-feet; the Milk river reservoir, 80,700 acre-feet; Raymond reservoir, 16,900 acre-feet; east Pothole reservoir, 14,000 acre-feet; and the Horsefly lake reservoir, 6,000 acre-feet.
Hon. members who have not been near a reservoir capable of storing thousands of acre-feet of water will have some difficulty in conceiving how large a project a reservoir of that size is. I can tell you that a reservoir such as the Pothole is not a duck pond; it is no puddle in the prairie. These are large reservoirs requiring huge dams. Even a reservoir capable of holding 6,000 acre-feet is quite large. Just where are you going to draw the line? Are you going to say that all these reservoirs down to the Raymond reservoir with 16,900 acre-feet are main reservoirs and the others are not? Really, all those matters should have been ironed out, and would have been if it had not been for the anxiety incident to the war.
There is one more reservoir that is of considerable importance. It is the Water ton river reservoir capable of storing 28,000 acre-feet. This one is not mentioned on page 181 of the Meek report, but it is mentioned by Walter Foss who was the engineer who designed the St. Mary dam. You will be able to find verification of that.
I shall continue my remarks when we reconvene.

Mr. Speaker, once again I should like to say a few words to show that I am opposed to these bills.
(Translation):
I wish, once again, Mr. Speaker, to protest against these divorce bills. It is a shame and a disgrace for representatives of the people who should protect the higher interests of their constituents, to act contrary to God's authority and contribute to the destruction of the family, that social entity upon which depends the life of nations.
Tonight, we are asked to approve these anti-Christian and anti-social measures, although we have not even looked into the false evidence submitted to the courts during the inquiries that preceded these decisions.
Marriage being indissoluble and of divine origin cannot be dissolved by man.
St. Matthew, chapter 19, from verse 3 on.
What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
In favouring divorce not only do we usurp a right which does not belong to us, but we bring down upon our country the wrath of Him who rules our destiny. Divorce is more than a calamity, it is national suicide. Its subversive character is a menace to society.
The more divorces we have in this country, the more children will roam the streets and the more inmates will there be in our prisons and penitentiaries.
The first victim of divorce is the child. He, more than any other, deserves our pity, for he is completely blameless of the evils that attend upon him and his misfortune leads to consequences less readily remedied than in the case of his parents. Parents can make a new start, as they say; not so the child. His home has been destroyed, and he is forevermore out of place.
Private Bills-Divorce
Divorce is, by its very nature, so inimical to childhood that it suppresses the child even before its birth.
In fact, the birth rate is lowest in countries where divorce is most prevalent. It is because of its socially disastrous effect that divorce must be condemned, since the advantage of any husband or wife cannot take precedence over the welfare of the community:
Disregarding the social repercussions of divorce would lead to a policy of compromise extremely detrimental to the maintenance of public order. Alleged termination, the Church notwithstanding, of a legal status assumed under its authority and auspices involves a dangerous responsibility.
In the general instructions which it issued to the Catholics of Canada in 1900, the first plenary council of Quebec stressed abstention:
In the above-mentioned divorce court, let the faithful abstain from behaviour which would be conducive to breaking the bond of matrimony.
That is why, as a Catholic and a true Canadian, I wish to do my duty by opposing such evil laws. I therefore beg the house to turn down these petitions.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to endorse the sentiments just expressed by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). I rise as a Protestant because I have the same feeling of revulsion as the hon. member has given voice to in passing these various divorce bills without due consideration. I feel humiliated that I should have sat here during the whole of the last parliament of Canada and on various occasions have seen twenty, thirty, forty or fifty bills asking for the relief of various individuals presented before this House of Commons. I wondered why these bills were presented to the House of Commons. I did not have the wisdom nor the courage to stand up on my feet and to ask why it is necessary that this type of bill should be passed through the House of Commons without any questions being asked. I say, and I am proud of the fact, that I am a member of the Church of England. I have always believed in the sanctity of the family. From my earliest boyhood I have felt that the British empire, now called the commonwealth, with Canada, has had all its history based upon the fact that the backbone of the nation was the unity and family life of the very humblest of her citizens, and therefore it has been extremely repugnant to me that I should be called upon to pass these bills for the relief of various individuals without a proper examination of the causes and reasons as to why the various individuals concerned are entitled to relief.

Private Bills-Divorce
I may be to blame. It may be that I should have examined more carefully the bills which had been passed in the other place. It may be that I should have attended some of the discussions of the committee which was investigating these matters. I plead guilty. I have not. It has been distasteful to me even to read the contents of the bills. It is seldom that I have done so. I have never attended any of the discussions in the committee; and while I plead guilty of having neglected perhaps my duty in that respect I know that the same negligence is true of practically every other hon. member. Very few of them have taken the time or have the time to sit in and hear the discussions of the various cases. I do not know whether it is possible for one to apply to some official of the house and have in printed form supplied to him the details with respect to the investigation carried out by that other body. Today there are about 100 new members sitting in the house, each and every one of whom will be asking himself the same question: What is this all about? Why am I called upon to sit on these chairs, like a bump on a log, and just say yea to a series of bills which, in my heart of hearts, I believe is striking at the very roots of our Canadian life, the sanctity of the home, the very thing upon which the backbone of this country has been built?
On this occasion, when within the last few weeks we have heard discussions with respect to crime comics, these matters are closer to our minds. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has introduced a bill in which he has regretted the prevalence of the crime comics being distributed throughout this land. That has focused attention from the Atlantic to the Pacific on this very question of the sanctity of the home.
Here is another invasion upon that great prerogative of British and Canadian peoples. Are we just going to accept these motions? Are we just going to pass them through? I would ask either the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or the hon. member who is introducing these bills, just why we should tender relief to John Henniker Torrance, or to Edith Harriet Black Hambly, or to Margaret Reid O'Connell, or to Alton Charles Bray.
Perhaps I should have found out these things, but with the exception of the hon. member who is sponsoring these bills, and possibly his seconder, I do not believe there is one member who is able to stand up and explain to us why we should grant relief to these particular individuals.
This whole matter is most repugnant to me. Perhaps someone will say: Why raise this question now? I have given one reason -because the country is being disturbed by attacks which have been made upon home

life through these crime comics, which have been brought to the attention of the whole country by such clubs as the Kiwanis clubs throughout Canada, and such organizations as the parent-teacher organizations, from one end of the country to the other.
This is one of the healthiest signs of today. There seems to be a determination from the Atlantic to the Pacific to preserve the Canadian home. It is therefore for that reason that I feel this is an opportune occasion to speak. Perhaps a minor reason which has come to my attention is that over this very week end, within a few miles of this city, services are being held to commemorate the visitation of that first great Protestant bishop, Jacob Mountain, who carried out his journeys throughout upper Canada almost two hundred years ago. In a small town between here and the St. Lawrence river people are gathering together to pay homage to that great missionary. If I have read correctly the biography of his life, no man in the history of Canada placed a higher valuation upon the home life of those early Canadian pioneers who settled, not only in upper Canada, but also in lower Canada, what is now known as the province of Quebec.
He was the great champion of the early life of the pioneers who settled here in Canada, people who came here perhaps as United Empire Loyalists after they had been driven out of what is now the United States. He was also the great champion of the French Canadians who were living in this land after the occupation. As a Protestant bishop he stood out and defended the rights of those people to worship in the way in which they had always been brought up to worship. He did not adopt a narrow point of view. The one thing which stands out all through his great life was that he was a champion of the sanctity of the home.
I feel therefore that today is an occasion upon which we may query the wisdom of passing carte blanche these numerous divorce bills. Then I was disturbed just the other day in this chamber-a week ago today to be exact-when, during a discussion of veterans affairs, some remarks were made regarding the possibility of veterans and their wives going to the United States and obtaining divorces there which would not be recognized in this country.
The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) made these remarks in reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South:
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) mentioned the matter of divorce. I do not know-
Order. The hon. member should not refer to another debate in the same session.

This took place during a discussion of the estimates a week ago. While perhaps I should not quote the actual words, the hon. member for Cape Breton South made it quite clear that there were difficulties experienced, so far as the veterans were concerned, where their wives might go over to the United States and there obtain divorces. In asking for a further explanation the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) asked if he -that is, the hon. member for Cape Breton South-really meant that he was advocating that veterans should be allowed to take common-law wives, and that such common-law wives would receive the allowances, if divorces were obtained?
Order. The hon. member should not refer to that debate at the present time.

Well, I am extremely sorry, Your Honour; but if I am not permitted to refer to it may I conclude by saying that I ivas perturbed by the levity with which the non. member for Yorkton said: "Well, if that is so, we would all get rid of our wives".

On a question of privilege, the member for Yorkton did not treat it with levity. He treated as serious the question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and assumed that if what he advocated did happen, that would be the effect. He considered as humorous that if that was the case some of us would get rid of our wives. The hon. member for Yorkton is just as good a family man, and probably better than the hon. member for Nanaimo.
I think probably this discussion will indicate to all hon. members that they should observe the rules.

I certainly am not going to enter into any discussion as to our relative family associations. I think I am capable of drawing the line between levity and humour. May I ask this question:	Is it indicative of
the general feeling which may be prevalent that perhaps the sanctity of the home is not regarded quite as highly as it used to be?
There is one other reason why I believe this question should be raised at the present time. We have welcomed into the brotherhood of Canada a tenth province, the province of Newfoundland. I am not learned in the law and I do not know anything about the divorce laws of that province, but I should like to know briefly what they are. Are we going to have a large number of bills presented for the relief of residents of our new province of Newfoundland?
I am in deadly earnest about this matter. I feel that this is a challenge to the times of today. As I said earlier, I plead guilty to the

charge of having failed to inform myself more fully about this matter, instead of passing these bills, in so casual and haphazard a manner throughout these years. I think the time has come when we might well ask why it is necessary that this House of Commons should have to deal with these bills, and also what will be the effect of this practice now that the tenth province of Newfoundland has been brought into this Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take part in a debate on the bill; I merely want to have the record straight. In view of the exchange between the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart), I feel that I must say something at this time. And in England too.

Some of these men remarried and they thought everything was all right until they came to apply for pension. They had gone through a legal ceremony, sometimes with the sanction of the church, but nevertheless the pension authorities did not consider them as being married. In so far as the bills themselves are concerned, may I say that I served on the committee for a couple of terms. I have always been opposed to the way this is done and have always suggested that some other means should be found of handling this matter. I think perhaps the exchequer court might be used, as I do not think it is too busy. But as long as the other place and the House of Commons want to do it this way, then I think it is entirely up to hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to register my objection to these bills, not because I object to divorce
