as such but because I object to the way they are presented here. First of all, I would point out that we have spent several days, as much as three hours on some days, discussing other private bills but so far this session these are the only private bills to my knowledge to which the government has not objected. Some of the other private bills which in my opinion were worthy of consideration were washed out because the government registered opposition.
We are being presented with a batch of forty-five private bills all sponsored by one member. Every one of these forty-five bills is couched in exactly the same language, the only difference being the name and the place of residence of the party concerned. There is no way in which I can have any knowledge of the merits of any one of these bills.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The hon. member gets the evidence.
Hon. members are being asked to pass en bloc forty-five bills about which they have no knowledge whatever, and to do that is simply to make a farce of this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is in the chamber because this matter is serious enough to be worthy of consideration, not only by the minister but by all members of the house. We have forty-five bills being presented under one motion for second reading, which of course has always been the practice. However, before the motion for second reading is passed I think we should have some assurance from the minister that consideration is being given to this problem. Each session hon. members have objected to the method in which these bills are handled, in fact have objected to parliament having to deal with divorce at all. I am confident that every hon. member here this evening who served in the last parliament is thoroughly disgusted with the whole procedure and is convinced that some new way should be found to deal with this question of divorce.
Protests have been made and agreement has been expressed on all sides of the house. It is not a party matter; it is a matter that concerns all of us as private members of the house. While there has been dissatisfaction nothing has been done about it. We are now in the first session of a new parliament, and I think it would be a great mistake to allow these bills to go through after a short discussion and a few complaints, and thereby establish a precedent which will be followed for the next four or five years of the life of this parliament.
IMr. Noseworthy.]
Therefore I hope that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has given consideration to a way to meet the problem, and that he can give us some definite assurance tonight that steps will be taken at an early date to get the whole problem out of the hands of parliament. It is most unfair in so many ways. First of all it is unfair to the unfortunate people concerned in the divorce actions. They have to pay far more to get a divorce in this way than they would pay to get a divorce before the courts. There is a great deal of delay. They can only get a divorce while parliament is in session. There is a great deal of publicity given to individual cases which would not be so before the courts. The transcript of the evidence taken before the committee of the other house is printed and distributed to every member of the House of Commons. I do not doubt that those transcripts become available to many people in Ottawa, and perhaps in other parts of Canada as well. The tragedies of the lives of these people are broadcast, which is a very objectionable feature, and a feature that is not allowed in some of the provinces. I know in the province of British Columbia the laws are very severe about what stories may be printed in the press arising out of divorce actions. From the point of view of the unfortunate individuals concerned, this method of obtaining a divorce is most objectionable, and I think entirely out of date.
From the point of view of the House of Commons the proceedings in connection with divorce bills are not judicial in any sense of the word. The House of Commons is not a court. We are not set up, and our committees are not set up, to try these cases as they should be tried. The procedure is wholly inefficient. It means a great waste of the time and energy of the members of the house. I believe the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) described it as a farce. He was quite correct in calling the whole procedure a farce. It is just one grand farce.
Worst of all, it is beneath the dignity of the House of Commons to have to deal with hundreds of divorce actions. I do not doubt that at this session several hundred of them will go through the mill at Ottawa. We were not elected to come down here to pass divorce bills. It is not our responsibility as members of the House of Commons. Therefore I hope that this new parliament will insist that some method be devised to deal with applications for divorce. Different solutions have been advanced-for example, the setting up of a new dominion court, or having the exchequer court expanded. Various other solutions have been suggested. I am not in a position to know which of them is the most workable,

but surely there is some way in which this problem can be met. I hope that the Minister of Justice, or one of the other ministers of the crown will explain to the house whether any legislation or plan is in contemplation that will meet the difficulty.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for at least the last fifteen years I have heard general debates on divorce in the House of Commons the first time that the bills were called for second reading. Sometimes I have participated in the debates. Tonight I thought I would remain quiet, but I have listened to the same speeches over and over again.
Not from me; this is the first time I have spoken.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, and I respect every word the hon. member uttered. I cannot agree with every word but I respect his opinion. I am the second member from the province of Quebec to speak on this question tonight. The hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) told the house and the country that for religious reasons and because of his convictions he was opposed to divorce. I agree with him; I am opposed to divorce. I should like the house not to forget that in everything I say in the few remarks I shall make that I am opposed and will always be opposed to, and will always vote against bills of divorce.
One hon. member rose and asked why it was that the government has allowed the house to discuss private bills for hours and hours since the beginning of the session and yet does not object to these divorce bills. If the hon. member will look over the orders since the beginning of the session he will see that so far we have not discussed one private bill. We have had public bills but we have not had private bills. I think he will see the difference between a public bill and a private bill.
Then there is the responsibility of members of parliament. The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) said that we were not elected to deal with divorce bills. I take issue with him on that point. If he will look up subsection 26 of section 91 of the British North America Act he will find that we have exclusive jurisdiction to legislate on divorce. No other body in the land has that jurisdiction.

If the minister will permit me, what I really meant to say was that our constituents did not believe when they elected us that they were electing us to come here to deal with applications for divorce.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member knows that his electors are all conversant with the British North America Act; they 45781-514
Private Bills-Divorce
know that this section is there, that it is the responsibility of this parliament. As to the history of divorce, Quebec is the only province where there are no divorce courts.
And Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Exactly; I inquired a moment ago about Newfoundland because I did not know.
That is why I asked the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Eight of the provinces have courts of divorce. Cases are heard, some are contested, but the majority are probably heard ex parte. I have read some of the evidence given before the courts and you will find that it is about the same evidence that is presented to the committee of the Senate charged with the duty of hearing it. There is not much difference. I have attended some of the sittings. The evidence is about the same, and the conclusions are the same. The only difference is that the house relies on what is done in the Senate. Our committee on private bills could call witnesses, and in the past we have called witnesses to have them repeat their evidence or enlarge upon it.
Eight of the provinces accepted courts of divorce. I think I know the sentiment of the province of Quebec, and I know that parliament would never try to impose divorce courts on that province. The great majority of the people do not believe in divorce or in courts of divorce. They do not even believe in this section of our constitution.
What is the position of parliament? We cannot hinder a person who desires to present a petition to parliament under this section of the British North America Act for the passing of a statute; and it must be remembered that each of these bills is a special statute passed just as we pass other statutes. We cannot deprive the citizens of this country of the right to petition parliament to have a bill passed. Then it is up to the houses of parliament to accept or reject these bills. Every time there has been a vote on these divorce bills they have been carried. In the ordinary course of our deliberations I have never seen them refused.

You have such a
majority.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend is fair in making that remark, because he knows that included in that large majority are about sixty-three coming from the province of Quebec, among whom there would not be very many who would vote for these bills.

Private Bills-Divorce
To answer the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, as to whether the government has been thinking of other means to replace this system, I can only say that in the last parliament consideration certainly was given to the question. Speaking from memory I believe a committee was even set up, composed of senators and members of parliament, to see if any new means could be devised to deal with these matters. When they began to study the question they realized the difficulties that confronted them, and they did not recommend any change in the present procedure. It was suggested that we might have a special court, a dominion court for divorces; that we might refer them to the exchequer court, and so on. Some even thought that we might accept the evidence given in Quebec as to separation of bed and board and permit that evidence to be used in divorce cases. Then we would become real rubber stamps, taking that evidence and passing bills based upon it. But that committee did not recommend any change in the present system, and no one who has spoken this evening has suggested any workable system that could be applied to the province of Quebec.
In my province we are satisfied with the way these bills are dealt with here. Oh, they do not like it, but they would rather have this system than have divorce courts in Quebec. So why should members elected from the other eight provinces try at every session to impose upon our province their way of dealing with marital cases? Some hon. members do not even know that Quebec is the only province in which divorce is not recognized.
And Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is true. In other days when I discussed this matter there was only Quebec; now there is also Newfoundland. If the people of those two provinces do not wish to have divorce courts, why should members from the other provinces try to impose that system upon them? I will vote against these bills; I am against them. Many people who favour divorce do not like this system. Well, let me tell you that none of the systems they have devised to separate man and wife are very good. I do not know of one that is worth very much. That is my personal opinion, not speaking as a member of the government.
These people have petitioned parliament; they have brought their evidence; the bills have been passed by the Senate and are here to be discussed. If they get second reading the principle is adopted, and then they go to a committee. That committee can get all the evidence it wishes before recommending that the bills be brought back to committee of the whole here, where they may be refused or

accepted. That is the system; and certainly if any of these bills are defeated it will not affect the government. We from Quebec probably would be pleased, because we do not like these divorce cases coming here or elsewhere.
I am not speaking for the government except when I reply to the hon. member who said the government did not oppose these private bills, but did oppose other private bills. Well, there were none until tonight; and the government does not interfere in these cases.

have been here about the same length of time as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), and each session during that period I think we have had a debate somewhat similar to the one we are having tonight. I believe we are dealing with this question in the wrong way. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) that we should not be condemning divorce as such, since divorce is recognized in every province of Canada with the exception of two, but rather we should be trying to devise some method of dealing with divorce cases from those provinces so that these people would not have to come to parliament and a statute be passed to deal with each separate divorce. That is the whole issue. I do not agree with those who say that the way divorce cases are dealt with in this parliament is a farce. I believe they are dealt with with just as much care, just as regularly and just as much in accord with the rules of evidence and procedure as they would be if heard in a court of law.
In the Senate; not in the House of Commons.

Yes, in the Senate. That brings up another point. Last year I discussed this question with some of the gentlemen in the other place and learned who were the members of the divorce committee. I found they were prominent lawyers, among others, all of them men of principles and judgment, men who believe in the institution of marriage. So these cases are dealt with according to established procedure. They come here as all other bills that originate in the other place; but we have reached the conclusion, and I think rightly-this was done many years before I came here-that there was no particular merit in discussing in this house what had been discussed thoroughly already in the other place where witnesses are sworn and evidence heard.
For some years I was on the miscellaneous private bills committee. I think all new members are put on that committee, though all new members could not go on it this time

because there are so many. As far as I can remember, during the four or five years I was on that committee there were only two cases in which the evidence was heard. The reason was that the committee was satisfied with the evidence as it came from the other place.
The Minister of Public Works says the people of his province are opposed to divorce. Evidently that does not apply to all the people of Quebec; otherwise we would have no divorce cases here. There is a minority in that province who believe in divorce; that is, they believe in divorce when there is no other solution to their family problems but the dissolving of the marriage contract. We speak about minority rights. I think there is here a definite minority right which should be recognized. Remember, no one has to present a petition for divorce, either to this house or to any court, if he or she does not want a divorce. There is no compulsion about it. Surely, people who believe that it is proper, in a legal manner, to dissolve the marriage and begin life over again are entitled to have some place to which they can appeal to that end.
The member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), for whom I have the very highest respect, has referred to the sanctity of the home. He has left the impression that it is the divorce that is destroying the sanctity of the home. Surely, that is all nonsense. The sanctity of the home is destroyed first, and the divorce is a result. The sanctity of the home is not going to be restored by refusing to grant a divorce. Let us be reasonable in this matter. Let us recognize that the people of Quebec and Newfoundland who want divorce are entitled to come to this parliament until such time as those provinces establish courts. If these provinces do not establish divorce courts there should be some dominion court to which they can come, not to destroy their homes, but to try to begin their lives over again. I think that is what most of the members of this house want.
In the province of Quebec, there is a way of dissolving a marriage. It is not called a divorce, but an annulment. In any event, there is a separation and the result is the same.
Oh, no.

The marriage is dissolved and the couple separate; that is the important thing. In common with many of the members here, I hope I will never need to appeal either to this parliament or to any other institution anywhere for a divorce. There are people, however, who will have to and it would, in many cases, perhaps be very difficult to place the blame on one party or the other. When the stage is reached when they cannot live
Private Bills-Divorce
together, the decent thing-I use the word "decent" in its proper meaning-is for them to separate. Nothing could be more indecent than that two people should have to live together after the love that brought them together had disappeared.

Many of us who are faced with this situation for the first time are certainly in a quandary in attempting to decide what we should do. I should like to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I also find these divorce bills very distasteful in more ways than one. I have all the trouble I want right at home without getting into any more. I should like, however, along with some of the others to express my opinion about some different form of making provision for these divorces that originate in provinces in which no divorce courts exist. If that were done, I would be relieved of the responsibility of passing judgment on something I do not know anything about.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, I am in a position where I just cannot vote. If I vote for the measure, I have to vote by taking someone else's word for it. It is not a proper procedure to follow. Perhaps all these bills should be passed, I do not know. Until I am in a position to say whether or not these bills should be passed, I am not in a position to say anything. With all deference to those who have spoken this evening, I have not heard sufficient reason yet for passing these bills. I should welcome some additional information, as I have no doubt the other new members would, as to how this procedure we follow came about.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (Si. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a subject upon which this house would be very strongly divided if it were a matter that was being introduced by the government. At the present time, I do not wish to go into the merits of the question of divorce. Some hon. members have made reference to the position in the province of Newfoundland, and it has now been made clear that we have no divorce law in Newfoundland. There are no divorce courts there. If anyone in Newfoundland wanted a divorce, he or she would have to come to parliament.
When one looks over this long list of persons, one thinks of the tragedies that must be wrapped up in these bills. I believe we should give some thought to this question of how these people came to be in that position. How could their lives be made happier, in the first place, and perhaps kept from going on the rocks? It seems to me that by providing an easy remedy such as divorce, we are not improving things for most of these people but making them worse. We all have sympathy with most of them, although we

Supply-Agriculture
know very little about the matter, as the previous speaker has said. It is difficult to form an opinion on the subject. I am happy to say that, up to now, we have no divorce in Newfoundland. I hope we will not have it.
I have had a good deal of experience in connection with domestic matters, as have some of the other members who come from Newfoundland. Both the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) and the member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Kent) have been magistrates and they know something about domestic cases in Newfoundland. I have taken a great interest in that subject. I have tried to talk to people and tried to get them to come to an agreement so that they would live happily together. It pleases me to be able to say that it worked. I believe if divorce were made easy, many of those families would have been broken up. I have seen men and women sitting in my office who seemed to hate one another. After talking it over with them, perhaps having them back again, I found that their differences disappeared. They went back together and lived happily, I hope, ever afterwards. In any event, they did not come back to me.

Special-
31. Major irrigation and water conservation projects in the prairie provinces, $7,500,000.

Before the house took recess, I was discussing the recent story of the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project, also called the St. Mary and Milk river conservation project. I told of the Meek committee formed in January, 1941, which submitted its report in February, 1942. They recommended an agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the province of Alberta before work began on this project. It was recommended by them that the dominion construct all works necessary to store Canada's share of the water. This committee recommended that Alberta should construct works to provide for the beneficial use of the water. I named the eight major reservoirs which constitute the project.
At this stage, I should like to name the six main canals which form part of the project. Those canals are listed on page 181 of the Meek report. The first one is the enlargement of the Taber canal; second, the canal

to the Medicine Hat district; third, the High Line canal across Chin coulee; fourth, the main canal to New Dayton district; fifth, the main canal to east Verdigris district; sixth, the main canal to Milk river district. There will be a good many other canals, some of which it will be difficult to classify as main or subsidiary.
Remembering what the committee said about the responsibility which it believed should be assumed by the federal government and the provincial government respectively, once more I say there will be room for considerable variance of opinion as between the federal authorities and the provincial authorities. I think it is fitting to observe that if any group of the hon. members who constitute this house found themselves responsible for the well-being of any one of the ten provinces in this dominion they would take their responsibilities very seriously and they would be careful not to assume any more financial commitments than were necessary under any given set of circumstances. I am sure that that would be true of the Minister of Agriculture himself, at one time premier of Saskatchewan. He must of course recognize that if a provincial government is worth anything to the province it will defend the interests of the province. The same is equally true of any group of gentlemen in this house who might be called upon to form a federal administration. They would be just as careful of the interests of the federal government, and it is just as natural that they would be. Bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, that the thing that I would resent, if I were to lend myself to resenting anything in connection with this very human situation, is this, that any one side should look upon the other as being culpable. That is not necessary. These groups of men are simply looking after the interests of the divisions of Canada for which they have the responsibility.
During the discussion of the disagreement which naturally will result from the situation which has developed, the main thing to be borne in mind by us and by the gentlemen who are charged with responsibility in each case is this: First there is water sufficient to iri'igate 345,000 acres of the finest land on the American continent. I speak as a member for the district and I know. That water is at stake. That water must be saved for generations yet unborn down through thousands of years if it is at all possible.
Let us not permit any subsidiary or minor or secondary consideration to dull our minds with respect to that point. The second major consideration which we must keep an eye on is this. If we are to save that water, if we are to prevent the United States from reclaiming it, for they are all ready to do so, we

must construct the various factors of that project with the utmost promptitude. There must be no delay whatsoever either on our part or on the part of any of the people charged with that responsibility.
The third thing to bear in mind is that the national value of the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project is such that it will justify the expenditure of all the money which is necessary to build the project by the federal government. Consequently no matter how much it entails-it may go over $25 million-every portion of this dominion should be fully aware that the money would be well spent and would be more than repaid, perhaps within twenty-five years, by the added wealth and production.
There are a good many people in the Dominion of Canada, especially those from Manitoba east, who are not in a position to be able to judge satisfactorily the value of this project as we are who come from the west and who know the conditions, especially those which obtain in what is known as the Palliser triangle. I think it would be doing a service for those hon. members if I were to put on Hansard, if I can have time to do so, the report of a committee which was appointed by the Engineering Institute of Canada. The document is called "Report of the Committee on Western Water Problems". The gentlemen who constituted that committee would all be Montreal men or easterners who would certainly look upon that project with critical and appraising eyes. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall read into the record from the report of this committee, which I think hon. members will be glad to be able to read. It gives a fine scientific summary of the whole case of the St. Mary and Milk river project as to facts, and suggestions based upon those facts, by a committee of men admirably fitted for the task they undertook.
Introductory to the report is this:
In 1935 the council of the institute appointed a committee under the chairmanship of G. A. Gaherty-
Whose name is familiar to, and much admired by, all hon. members.
-to study the problem of water distribution in the drought area of the western provinces. Subsequently a subcommittee was appointed and between these two bodies a great volume of work has been accomplished. At the annual meeting in Ottawa in 1939 eight papers were presented on this subject as part of the work of the committee. Herewith is the complete report which was presented to council on January 18, 1941.
I am not going to read the complete report, Mr. Chairman; I am going to read merely those parts which will be of particular interest to hon. members, and anyone who desires to have the original report may come and get
Supply-Agriculture
it from me. I shall gladly let him read it. I read from the report of the subcommittee:
Your committee submits:
1.	That the St. Mary and Milk rivers are international, that their waters are now partially used and can be fully used, beneficially, mainly for irrigation, but also, to some extent, for domestic and other purposes, by Canada and the United States together.
2.	That the division of the waters between the two countries is governed by a treaty between Great Britain and the United States, dated January 11, 1909, and under the supervision of a permanent authority, the international joint commission.
3.	That the international joint commission, after holding hearings over a period of about six years, made rulings under date of October 4, 1921, as to the methods of determining the allotment to each country, and on October 6, 1921, made certain recommendations regarding provision of storage reservoirs.
4.	That either country may, for good and sufficient cause, ask for a reopening of the matter and request modification of the regulations in its interest.
5.	That since October 4, 1921, the waters have been divided between the two countries in accordance with the rulings, but that there has been no joint action with regard to storage.
6.	That Canada's share of the waters of the two rivers allotted to her under the terms of the treaty as interpreted by the regulations of the commission has averaged since 1922 about 393,000 acre-feet annually.
7.	That Canada has been diverting and putting to beneficial use since 1935 an average of about 172,000 acre-feet annually, from the natural unregulated flow of the St. Mary river and not more than 2,000 acre-feet annually from Milk river.
8.	That Canada's share, still unused, amounts to an average of about 220,000 acre-feet annually.
9.	That the government of the United States has been and is proceeding diligently to use its share of the water of the two rivers. That works now constructed, in progress or contemplated are adequate to put to beneficial use all of its share and more.
10.	That the general principle governing the right to the use of water for irrigation and other uses, in arid and semi-arid areas, is its application to beneficial use.
11.	That, as a consequence, Canada, if she fails to exercise due diligence in putting her share to beneficial use, stands in danger of losing, in perpetuity, valuable rights allotted to her under the terms of the treaty.
12.	That there is an economically sound method of beneficially utilizing Canada's share of these international waters.
13.	That this utilization will create taxable wealth and a flow of trade far in excess of the cost.
14.	That the utilization of this water in irrigating available lands will bring about an extension of intensive agriculture into one of the worst drought areas, a very desirable contribution to full national and provincial development, and a very substantial contribution to the solution of the perennial problems of drought, crop failure and relief costs.
With respect to the specific problems of water utilization, your committee finds:
1.	That it is economically desirable to associate the full development of the St. Mary river and the Milk river with plans for their common development with the waters of the Belly and Waterto rivers.
2.	That it is quite feasible and relative!, simple to carry the available waters of the Belly and Water-ton rivers into the St. Mary river at a point between Cardston and Spring Coulee.

Supply-Agriculture
That is right where the St. Mary dam now is.
3.	That it is feasible to create a storage reservoir of approximately 270,000 acre-feet capacity on the main channel of St. Mary river near Spring Coulee and below the point of inflow of the water diverted from the Belly and Waterton rivers.
4.	That the proposed reservoir is ideally situated in that it will control the entire annual flow of St. Mary river below any important tributary, and that, together with the diverting works, canals and auxiliary reservoirs, it can conserve for beneficial use all of the available water of these three rivers, an estimated average of 760,000 acre-feet annually.
5.	That after allowing for 210,000 acre-feet for lands already having irrigation rights, this amount of water will be sufficient to serve an additional area of 345,000 acres.
6.	That there is an area of tributary land suitable for irrigation and intensive agricultural development very substantially in excess of the above area, which has been designated as the Lethbridge South East Project.
7.	That the proposed development is economically feasible and is definitely related to national provincial and local growth and self-sufficiency.
8.	That climatic and soil conditions of the areas available for irrigation development are similar to those of the Lethbridge area. That crops that it is known can be grown to advantage under irrigation include alfalfa and other forage crops, sugar beets, potatoes, vegetables, and some fruits and coarse grains (as well as wheat), all of which lend themselves to building up intensive agricultural production and are important adjuncts to the livestock industry on adjacent grazing lands, as is so well exemplified in the present irrigated areas around Lethbridge and in other irrigated areas of the semiarid region.
9.	That there will be some important structures of large-but by no means unprecedented-size, and that the very considerable investigations already made indicate that there will be no serious foundation or other construction problems.
10.	That the completed project will cost about

Of course hon. members realize that that was a 1939 figure. It would probably be twice that much, or probably more, today- -or not more than $40 per acre of irrigable land. That it lends itself to an orderly step-by-step development over a period of years. That its construction, in considerable measure, will lessen relief costs during the construction period and will thereafter result in the transfer of many farmers in the drought area from relief rolls to self-supporting, wealth-producing agriculturists.
Your committee recommends that the Council of Engineering Institute of Canada should, through the proper channels, suggest:
1.	That the dominion and provincial governments, in co-operation, approve the development of the Lethbridge South East Project and constitute an agency for carrying out such development. That funds be made available for an early start on construction in accordance with a plan for orderly progress over a suitable period.
2.	That an agency charged with development should, before final decisions are made with respect to important engineering structures and system layout, appoint an advisory board of engineers and at least one geologist to report on sites, foundations and designs.
3.	That the same or another advisory board of engineers and economists be appointed to report on the joint engineering and economic aspects of the project.

4.	That in the interest of allocating unused water to the best advantage, the province of Alberta set up an advisory board to study this matter and advise the government. That pending the results of such procedure, action on applications for allotment of unappropriated water be deferred as far as possible.
I think that is sufficient to give hon. members from eastern Canada a chance to appraise this project satisfactorily. I thought it would be a good thing to put these quotations on the record, as support for the Minister of Agriculture. I fancy that the minister's lot constitutes no bed of roses, when he endeavours to get financial support for these irrigation schemes. He will require all the support he can get. I can think of no document I have come across which will give that support more effectively than this one I have just read.
To hon. members I wish to express appreciation of the committee for listening so courteously to me while I have given this outline. May I once more urge that throughout all the, what one might call, human bickerings which might go on between the Alberta and the federal governments, while they are struggling to protect the interests of the bodies to whom they are responsible, we shall all keep our eyes on the ball; and the ball is, first of all, that there is enough water to irrigate 345,000 acres of the finest land to be found on the continent of America. That water will keep on for hundreds of years, for the benefit of Canadians yet unborn. If we lose that water we lose a priceless heritage for those same generations yet unborn.
We must also keep in mind, while we struggle, that we have no time to waste, and that this project must be proceeded with, with the utmost promptitude. No matter what this project may cost to build- and it will not be unduly unreasonable-we shall find, I am sure, within twenty-five years, that the added wealth which will come to Canada through the building up of this project will more than repay us in revenue over and above the expenditures we shall have to lay out to build the project.

The date is 1942. I do not believe that the committee assumed that anyone was going to be held to the absolute percentages that were indicated. All that has been suggested by the federal government is that we should follow the recommendation of the Meek report and that, on the basis of present conditions, we should revalue the requirements necessary to carry out the project, which is a much bigger thing than just the development of the St. Mary dam and the waters that will be available from the St. Mary dam. What I maintained last night was that in discussions since the report was made it had been agreed between ourselves and the Alberta government that at some time or other-and the agreement was made while we were still under conditions where it was impossible to have construction because of war-we were going to sit down and agree on a division which would be based in principle upon what has been said in the report. We have had a table made up which shows that if you were to follow exactly what is indicated in the report, that is, if you were to follow the exact reservoirs which they say are federal or which they suggest might be federal, under present conditions, and divided up the same way, the cost to the dominion would be

All we have said is, in view of the fact a table was set up which suggested a certain division on the ground that division at the time might result in about a fifty-fifty apportionment of the cost, and in view of the changes that have taken place as a result of the fact that we had four years of war since the report was made and we have had new conditions resulting from the war, that when we sit down to reconsider the position this is a basis from which we might start. Our objective would be to get it as close as possible to a fifty-fifty basis with the same conditions placed upon it as the commission recommended, namely, that some of the money could be collected from the farmers, but that none of that money so collected would accrue to the federal government. Anything that might be collected would accrue to the provincial government.
All we say about that is that we want to know what that collection is going to be in order that we may be satisfied, before we put $15 million into a project, that the farmers are going to be able to live on the land and finance themselves after that collection is made. No other suggestion has been made. Some people think that we have been a long time getting together. The present position is that we have been discussing proposals made by the province and they have been considering proposals made by us. We think we are pretty close to the time when we can reach an agreement. I have been a little concerned, as well as the hon. member for Lethbridge, that in our discussions we should not get into a position where misunderstandings might be created where there are none now, and where there have not been any.
As a matter of fact the government of Alberta have always acknowledged, in any discussions I have had with them, that irrigation is a provincial responsibility. They have never questioned it, but they have said that no matter how much it is a provincial responsibility there is no way they can raise all the money that is necessary in order to take care of the cost, which at the time the Meek report was made was $43 an acre for land, and which today at present rates is $70 an acre for land. The province naturally says that even if it were their responsibility, and if the federal government were to say that they would not assume any obligation in connection with it, they just could not go on with the project at all.
We understand that, and all that has been suggested up to the moment is that we follow the same principle that was recommended in

I hope that the discussion will at least have thrown some light on the matter.

must come from the nation's credit. The main problem is to get the parliament of Canada to approve the expenditure of $66,360,000.
On a $100 million project.

It said that it must be a national project. I come to the speeches my right hon. friend made just a year ago,- the first on October 16, 1948, during the by-election in Rosthern.
I asked the minister a few moments ago whether, in the event that the province would not supply the necessary money for this irrigation project, the dam would be gone ahead with as a power project-in other words, to provide for industrialization.
You are asking a hypothetical question which will not happen. But Saskatchewan will have a government which will assist.
Oh, but that was not the view last year, as I shall read.
It might even be a government under your new leader you have just come back from choosing.
It is all very well for the minister to say that. If promises had been made by us they would have been carried out; and when the minister makes a promise the people take him at his word.
That is because for thirty-five years I have always carried out any promises I made.

Then I am asking the minister now to continue what he says has been his practice for thirty-five years. That is the very reason I am bringing this to his attention-and by his interruptions he is not diverting me from reading his promises.
I take this from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
Great Industrial Development Seen if Big Dam Built
Unexpected industrial development would follow construction of the proposed Outlook dam, Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner told the annual meeting of the Saskatoon Liberal Association, Thursday night. The federal agricultural minister predicted that the dam would furnish electric power for a wide farming area as well as providing irrigation for many acres. It would mean a changing economy for this sector of the province, he said.
Under the heading "His Main Job" the article continues:
Mr. Gardiner said his main task in the commons- as well as that of W. A. Boucher, if elected, in the Rosthern by-election-would be to "push the building of the dam as much as possible." . . . "The time has come when we must put great emphasis on the development of this country," Mr. Gardiner declared.

And then a little later, on October 22, 1948, we find this in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
The fact that two federal cabinet ministers have expressed a favourable attitude toward the south Saskatchewan river irrigation and power project in the Rosthern by-election campaign has contributed to make this one of the main campaign issues, Walter Tucker, Saskatchewan Liberal leader, declared at a public meeting here Thursday night.
Mr. Tucker said that it is "now up to the people of Rosthern to give their endorsement by electing William A. Boucher, Liberal candidate-
Hear, hear.
A good man. They elected him, too.

Yes, they did. It continues:
-if they want the project proceeded with."
You may applaud that.
He added, "You certainly won't get anywhere by sending C.C.F.'ers to Ottawa:	the election of
Makaroff would be tantamount to repudiation of the great scheme."
"We have now reached the stage where public opinion will have to be mobilized behind the project to help obtain the passage through parliament of the necessary funds." Mr. Tucker continued, "it is imperative for the people of Rosthern to send Mr. Boucher to Ottawa to help Mr. Gardiner in his fight for it."
Hear, hear.
You have a cheering section now.
You ought to read one of your own speeches.
I appreciate the help from all quarters of the house.
And you need it, too.

It continues:
The fact that the Hon. Paul Martin, Minister of National Health and Welfare, had shown a favourable attitude toward the project while he participated in the by-election campaign, was construed by Mr. Tucker as evidence that advocates of the project were making headway in winning converts in the east.
Then on October 21, 1948, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix carries the headline "Outlook Dam Would Mean Development of Heavy Industry in West Canada", and states.:
Development of irrigation and power on the south Saskatchewan river by means of the Outlook dam would mean industrial and agricultural development of western Canada similar to the Essen country of Germany.
In another report appearing in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of October 23, 1948, under the heading "Immense Benefits from Dam," it is stated that:
In a speech Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner said, "If this part of the country could be turned into an industrial as well as an agricultural area, it would be possible for it to support twice the population that it does now."
Did you not say all that, and a lot more, in your speeches?
Surely, I said it. And I am asking for the construction of the dam so that we can industrialize Saskatchewan. That is the reason I am asking for it.
You will never be in power to do it; we will be.

Would the hon. member
permit a question from an Ontario member?
Would the hon. member sit down?
Then I shall ask it when he has finished.
What was the interruption?
Will he ever get through?
I had a question to ask, but the hon. member would not answer it. I shall ask it later on.

The article continues:
Cheap power is the open sesame to industrial growth. With a dam at its back door almost assured, and with the resultant cheap water power available in the not too distant future, Saskatoon stands at the gateway to new and unprecedented development.
I could go on and read further references from the speeches made by my right hon. friend, all of which point out the necessity for power development in our province, with incidental irrigation development. I say to him this, that if we in that province now are to find ourselves in the position where the dam is not to be proceeded with unless the provincial government says that it will spend several million dollars a year to take up 50 per cent or thereabouts of the irrigation costs then, sir-
Why shouldn't you?
Stick to the Fraser valley.

We supported the hon. member last year when he was advocating assistance for the Fraser valley at the time of a national disaster. Saskatchewan is losing population. We have 70,000 less in that province now than we had in 1936. This project represents the hope of the people of that province, and it is for that reason that I defend it in this House of Commons.
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is a good friend of mine- a personal friend. He will admit this, that British Columbia paid 25 per cent of the cost of that expenditure.

I do not argue that point at all. But I am arguing this, that so far as
Supp ly-A griculture
a dam is concerned to produce the necessary power to be made available for industrialization, we in the province of Saskatchewan have the right to expect that this project will be proceeded with nationally.
When the minister was answering the hon. member for Moose Jaw I could not believe that he was placing before this committee his considered view that this project, which represents so much to hundreds of thousands of people in our province, is to be placed in a position where its construction, instead of being a national undertaking, is to be an undertaking in part national and in part provincial.
The minister distributed a map when he spoke in Saskatoon, showing the benefits of this project. When he spoke, he raised no question at any time that this project was going to be dependent upon whether or not the water would be actually utilized for irrigation purposes. He placed before the people of Saskatoon, in that address before the board of trade, the benefits which would follow in keeping in Saskatchewan the thousands who are leaving that province.

My hon. friend should
attend some of my meetings because-
May I ask the hon. member a question?
My hon. friend should attend some of my meetings because I have never made an address on this subject without calling attention to the fact that the province has some obligation.
The press did not report it?
They reported it once. Anything that has been said half a dozen times is not news any longer.
They did not report it once.
They reported it when it was necessary to report it. It was always understood.
May I ask the hon. member for Lake Centre if at any time in the history of Saskatchewan he went around and said that the minister had let Saskatchewan down?
Mr. Chairman-
I should like that question answered.

My hon. friend asks a question that has nothing whatever to do with this matter. It is not pertinent, and the kind of question one would expect the hon. gentleman to ask.

Supply-Agriculture
Very smart.

Having said that, may I say that I am surprised at the attitude taken by the Saskatchewan members in opposing my endeavour to get this for Saskatchewan. I am surprised at the attitude they take when I bring this matter before the committee. Each of them said during the campaign that he was in favour of it. Now when I endeavour to impress upon the minister the necessity of something being done if the morale of the people is to be maintained, they oppose my efforts. The people have been looking forward to this. Two years ago the minister said that within two years the government would decide on the location of the dam and the work would proceed at the earliest possible moment. The last time the matter came before the house the minister said that they were going to continue the investigation. There was never a word when the matter came up that this great project was going to be placed in jeopardy because part of the responsibility in regard to irrigation was going to be imposed upon the provincial government. What I am saying this evening, and I shall say no more-
Hear, hear.

That is the best contribution my hon. friend has ever made. I have requested the minister to join with those hon. members from Saskatchewan who have been interrupting me when I have been making this argument and impressing upon this committee and the country, as it no longer needs to be impressed, that this is a national project, necessary for our province if its population is to be maintained. I shall not enter into an argument as to whether there should be a division of responsibility between the dominion and the province, because then each will endeavour to pass the buck to the other. The people of the province do not want any of that. They are asking that this national work be proceeded with.
During the days of the war hundreds of millions of dollars were spent in other provinces to lay an industrial foundation. We in Saskatchewan got none of that. I thought we were all united in this regardless of party considerations. I thought we all wanted to rebuild our economy to the end that the exodus of our people would be restrained by the industrialization which was pictured in two or three of the minister's addresses when he pointed out that there were great possibilities in the way of power to industrialize the province and change its economy to such an extent that a livelihood would be pro-

vided for the many thousands of people who today find it necessary to leave because of drought and climatic conditions.
It is in that spirit that I make this appeal. I am not entering any arguments as to whether it is a provincial or dominion obligation. All I know is that all our people believed that the minister had the authority to make the promise he did when he said that this would be proceeded with without delay. This is not a political matter in the province. All are united in this. The Liberal members to my right were elected in its support. The C.C.F. candidates spoke in favour of it. No one in the province has dared within the last two years to stand up and say that he did not fully support going ahead with this project.
I think hon. members of this committee are willing to give our province assistance in this regard, assistance which will spell an improvement in our economy and above all stop that exodus which is reducing Saskatchewan year by year to a lower and lower position in the population category of the provinces of this dominion. It is in that spirit that I approach this matter. Our people as a whole are going to be intensely disappointed-
Nobody has said that there is going to be any stoppage.
May I ask a question from a non-partisan point of view?
That is why I know the question will be non-political.
How many people in Saskatchewan thought on June 27 that the official opposition represented the people of Canada?
On October 27, 1948-
June, I said.

On October 27, 1948, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix contained this editorial:
The Liberal campaign was based in large part on the promotion of the south Saskatchewan river development, the project that offers the quickest bargain in national dividends anywhere in the country and which needs only the approval of the Canadian parliament. . . The Liberal victory represents a decisive endorsation of the south Saskatchewan river development.
Another excerpt from an editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of October 26, 1948, reads:
The election was fought on a number of issues; the Liberals seeking endorsement of their agriculture and social security policies and asking support for a large irrigation project on the south Saskatchewan river.

That was the issue a year ago in that by-election. During the federal election no issue was made of that because we all believed that the project was to be proceeded with. I say once more that there is going to be the greatest disappointment in Saskatchewan over the minister's announcement. I have nothing more to say because the government with its majority can determine whether or not this work will be proceeded with.

Will the hon. member permit a question from an Ontario member? I think the hon. member will concede that there are members in this house other than those from Saskatchewan like himself who are interested in the welfare of Saskatchewan. I listened with a great deal of interest to the plan outlined by the minister whereby the federal government would assume roughly fifty per cent of the total cost of this tremendous project that means so much to Saskatchewan. I learned also that the remaining portion of the cost would be borne by the province and those who would directly benefit, such as the farmers and those who would be using the electric current which would be developed. I suggest to the hon. member for Lake Centre that if he wants to advance the project he will get a lot further with the other members of the house in doing so if he will argue to the point, tell the members of the house what he does not like about the program, and make his own suggestions as to what would be a fair and equitable distribution of the cost. He will get a lot further than by making -and I say this in all sincerity-smart-aleck answers to questions from members who are honestly seeking to get his views.
What is your question?
In what way does the hon. member for Lake Centre object to the broad proposals outlined by the minister?

First may I say that I have always noticed in this house a fine spirit of co-operation among members in appreciating the difficulties of other parts of the country. My experience has never been that there is in this country an east working against a west. I often hear that in the west, but I have never found it to exist. There is that spirit that was displayed a moment ago by the hon. member in his very studied, careful and objective remarks. I want to say that I have set forth what the promises were and what the people are asking.

If I may be permitted, I have listened carefully to the entire speech of the hon. member.
Supply-Agriculture
He does not like it.
He read some excerpts, but he did not give me any idea of what he thought was unfair about the broad outline given by the minister as to how the cost of this tremendous project is to be borne.
You had better read it in Hansard.

I am not going to make any prepared observations. I should like the hon. member for Lake Centre to tell us if it is his view, and the view of the people resident in his province, that the whole cost of the project should come from the consolidated revenues of the Dominion of Canada. I have in mind that some of this type of work is being done in the province of British Columbia. Water is being provided to a certain point, but that water is being collected with one end in view, and that is land use. The water is no good unless you use it and it is being used on land. Certainly our provincial government is going to co-operate with the federal authorities in the distribution of that water at Westbank, and again on the west bench at Penticton in particular. They are certainly going to co-operate with the federal government, and are co-operating right now in respect of the work at Pemberton. I can visualize there is only one source from which the money comes, and that is revenues collected from all parts of Canada. If the people of Saskatchewan are going to take the stand that the people of all parts of Canada must bear 100 per cent of the cost of the project in Saskatchewan, I am afraid you are going to have a difficult time selling that idea to the people of British Columbia.
Hear, hear.
I will deal with my friend in a moment. He is an authority on hardware.
Not even on that.

And the Regina manifesto, but he is not an authority on soil fertility. I remember that last year $167 million was collected from the province of British Columbia by the federal government. I wonder how much came out of Saskatchewan. If we are going to take these projects on a national basis, as we certainly must, and along the lines outlined by the minister and by the hon. member for Lethbridge, then there is justification for them on the basis that they will keep more people in Canada and produce more wealth which will be distributed all over Canada. That is the only justification for them. It seems to me if the people of a certain province are going to take the stand that they will contribute nothing and that

Supp ly-A griculture
they want everything from Ottawa, it is in the interests of the Dominion of Canada to know that right now.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussions that have taken place regarding the St. Mary river and south Saskatchewan projects. I realize how important it is that a satisfactory understanding be reached as to the St. Mary river project because the minister has stated that the agreement that is signed for that project will be the pattern for all future contracts. Therefore if we get off on the wrong foot on the first project we will have a problem with the rest.
I want to ask a few questions about the Red Deer irrigation project because that is included in this item. Two reservoirs have been created on Berry creek, and I understand that two more are under construction this year, one further south on Berry creek and one on Sounding creek. I should like to say that the farmers in those areas appreciate very much the fact that the government has constructed those dams. On the other hand, they also realize the fact that these reservoirs are absolutely dependent upon surface runoff of water for their supply. Consequently in years when there is no runoff there will be no water available for irrigation. For example, take the dam that was constructed last year in that reservoir. There is not enough water there now to drown a mouse, for the simple reason that there is no runoff. Therefore the people of that area feel that they will never have the assurance of irrigation until such time as the main project is constructed under which water will be diverted from the Red Deer river into Hamilton lake, and from there down through the drainage creeks into various parts of that land.
The first dam that was built was the Bartman dam which was built several years ago on Berry creek. That project provides for irrigation by gravity and many hundreds of acres have been irrigated from that reservoir. Good use has been made of it. The other three dams that have either been built or are being built are for the purpose of creating reservoirs to provide water for irrigation by means of a sprinkler system.
The question I should like to ask the minister is what the policy of the federal government is with regard to providing grants to farmers for the purchase of aluminum pipe in connection with the sprinkler system. I sat down with the chairman of the special areas board and discussed the matter with Mr. Larry Helmer, who is the P.F.R.A. agent at Hanna. He told us that a grant of $350 per farmer would be provided for the purpose of buying aluminum pipe for

irrigation projects provided that no money had been given to those farmers for the purpose of digging dug-outs or erecting dams. I am especially interested in finding out whether or not that is correct. I do not doubt it because the minister knows the man to whom I refer. I know him well and I know he is not the type of man who runs around making irresponsible statements. Therefore I take it that it is correct.
The reason I am interested is that if irrigation is going to be provided by a sprinkler system it will mean a great saving in cost to both the federal and the provincial governments in not having to dig ditches. If the federal government is making a grant I think there is every reason why the provincial government would also make a contribution towards a sprinkler system because such a system would also save them the cost of digging ditches for the purpose of getting water on the land. Another reason why we favour a sprinkler system in that area is that it is rolling land and it will not be easy to irrigate by means of ditches. Secondly there is a certain amount of alkali, and with a sprinkler system we will not have so much trouble. I know many people will say that a sprinkler system is far more expensive than a gravity system. I listened to Dr. Palmer from the Lethbridge experimental farm, however, who showed clearly that while the initial cost may be greater, nevertheless over a period of time it would be even cheaper than a gravity system because there would be such tremendous savings in labour. So I wonder if the minister could briefly outline the policy in regard to the purchase of aluminum pipe.

I believe the hon. gentleman asked me this question earlier in the session, and I was unable to answer it until I communicated with the western organization. They tell me no such suggestion has ever been made. They say some of the agents selling aluminum pipe promoted the sale of the pipe on the basis that the government ought to do this. Anyone who is familiar with suggestions of that kind realizes that you do not have to go very far-as a matter of fact you need not go outside this house, if you look at the newspaper reports-to have a suggestion by an agent selling something become a suggestion that the government ought to do something, and finally have someone saying the government is going to do it. The government have never said they are going to do it. As a matter of fact we had six men out this summer investigating the position with respect to that kind of irrigation, and we have not sufficient information to advise farmers to adopt it as against some other methods. It does not settle all those

problems having to do with alkali, and so on; we know that. Those matters are associated with the amount of water and the manner in which it is put on the land. An individual might put water on his land by means of pipes and cause damage through alkali, just as he might cause the damage in some other way.
Most of the reservoirs that have been constructed in the vicinity of Hanna are of a type and in a position which will make it possible to utilize them in connection with the Red Deer project when it is brought into being. They were built as the result of representations made by a delegation that came from Hanna to Lethbridge when I was there in 1947, I think, or the early part of 1948. Their representations were to the effect that if those reservoirs were proceeded with while the other larger project was under consideration, in the meantime it would be possible for them to irrigate some six or seven thousand acres of land. I brought those representations back here and recommended to the government that we proceed with those reservoirs, and following that recommendation the work was carried on.
The unfortunate thing about it, and what makes it possible for the hon. member to say there was not enough water in some of these reservoirs this year to drown a mouse, is that there was no rain. That is the reason we have irrigation systems out west. I may tell my hon. friend that I built a very large cistern on my own farm, which is in a district that usually has much more moisture than most of the constituency my hon. friend represents. While I have a barn roof 100 feet long and 40 feet wide from which to get water for the cistern, which is only 10 feet wide and 60 feet long, I have not had more than 20 inches of water in it at any time this year. The fact is that we did not have three inches of rain from one July to the next. That is why we talk about irrigation out west. It does not rain enough every year to put water into the reservoirs. But we are hopeful that in the years to come we will have runoffs some time, and when we get those reservoirs filled they will take care of the needs over considerable periods of drought. Then when we get the larger scheme in operation these reservoirs will be filled from time to time from the larger dams.
After having said this, I do not want anyone to say that I made the promise tonight that we are going to build the dam at some particular time. I am only saying that when that dam is constructed-and I assume it will be constructed-the reservoirs which have been put in this year will form part of the whole system and it will not be necessary
Supply-Agriculture
to have them supplied by runoffs every year. The water will be brought in from the larger reservoir that will be put in for the purpose of replenishing these smaller ones from time to time.
I think the minister misunderstood me. I did not say a salesman for a particular system had said anything.

I know my hon. friend did not say that; he referred to somebody I knew very well. I do not really know whom he is talking about, but likely I do know the man very well; I know a great many people in Alberta very well. I am saying that we investigated that rumour, it led us back to the salesmen who were selling pipe. They were going around that district saying these things, and I have no doubt somebody believed what was being said, and it was not long until someone said the government was going to do it. Well, we are not doing it.

I can give the minister the name of the person responsible for the rumour. He is the district representative of P.F.R.A., Mr. Larry Helmer. He gave that information to the chairman of the special areas board, and I was there when it was given. That information was also given to the east central irrigation association; and keen enthusiasm in the sprinkler system has been created throughout the district by the minister's own representative.

The director, who is sitting in front of me, tells me Mr. Helmer is the very man he investigated out there, and that was where he got the information that these statements were being made by the agents. When they told him that he took it for granted the information was correct, and repeated it.
Then I would suggest that the minister immediately contact Mr. Helmer, because the sooner that rumour is denied the better it will be. Otherwise it may cause a great deal of trouble.

I took it up with the director right after my hon. friend mentioned it to me, and he tells me that he contacted Mr. Helmer and that what my hon. friend suggests has been done. I am quite sure he is not circulating that report now.

I am glad to hear that. I am not saying this was done during the election campaign. As a matter of fact that information was given to us six weeks after the election, so I am not making any charge of political propaganda. I should like to ask the minister one or two other questions. Could he say whether or not consideration has been given by the prairie provinces water board to the construction of the Red Deer diversion project?

Supply-Agriculture

I am informed that up to the present the Alberta government has not applied to that board for a diversion of water for the Red Deer project. I am not saying this to be critical of that government. The understanding we have with the government of Alberta is that the Bow river project, which was under way, would be proceeded with by the federal government with as little as possible in the way of further discussions with the province. They assumed that we had undertaken the obligation and would go along with it until we reached the point of working the land they owned, and that then the matter would be discussed and we would come to some arrangement about it; and we intend to come to that arrangement. Then they agreed that after this the St. Mary project should be proceeded with and developed as rapidly as possible, and that the Red Deer project should follow after that. So we have been devoting the greater part of our time and effort to the first two projects. With respect to the other one, in the meantime we have been making these temporary arrangements and putting in small dams that do take care of some of the farmers.
Did I understand the minister to say the St. Mary river project would be completed first, and then the Bow river project?
Perhaps I should not say it will be completed. We intend to get it far enough under way so that it is a going concern, and then turn our attention to the other project.
I am glad to hear that, because it means we will not have to wait another fourteen years.
That is right.

I am fortunate in representing a constituency in Saskatchewan where we do not need irrigation, but I have been interested in this discussion. In that province we are all interested in the irrigation project, and particularly in industrialization. When the minister stated, as I think he did, that the government would be responsible for the major work, that is the dam for storing the water, and that the province would come into the picture in the distribution of the water and the irrigation of the land, so far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned I believe that has been understood. Last year a department of the provincial government was set up to make a study of irrigation and to be prepared, if and when the dominion government completed the dam, to do something with the water. We hope they (Mr. Quelch.]
will not have to wait ten years to get some water to us. I think they will be prepared to use it before that.
I am interested in this point: If the dominion government is going to build the major dams, then will the dominion government own the power which will result from that dam? It seems to me that is an important point. Who is going to own the power that will be produced at the major dams? Will it be under the control of the province or under the control of the dominion? If the dominion is building the dam and will own the power, then it will be able to get large returns from the power. I should like to hear the minister's explanation of that situation.

I am pleased to hear the hon. member who comes from the northern part of Saskatchewan, an area that is not concerned really with this particular development, say that the province was assuming an obligation in connection with this project and has set up an organization to take care of this obligation. That is right. There is another development which has never been discussed in this house to any great extent and which I am not going to start discussing at this time of night, which does not happen to be within the bounds of either Alberta or Saskatchewan, but which will serve the northern part of the province. Even though the hon. member comes from a section of the province which is some distance from where these discussions have taken place, I was pleased to hear what he said.
This government has been assuming that the water which is put there for the purpose of irrigation and the purpose of power will be utilized by the province or some agency set up under provincial law. Irrigation law is provincial law. As my hon. friend knows, I had the privilege of setting up the power commission in the province of Saskatchewan. It is still operating. It is the expectation of this government that the power commission will utilize the power. It is not the intention of the government to charge rates for water, either for power purposes or for irrigation purposes, which will return part of the capital cost. If anything is charged it will only be enough to pay for the maintenance of the dam and the reservoir that holds the water. This subject has been discussed here and it was agreed by all that there should only be a charge of that kind.
If the discussion is to be continued until eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I shall carry on, but if it is the desire of the committee to call it eleven o'clock now, I am agreeable.
Carry the item.

I had hoped, sir, that I was merely going to speak on the smaller project which, in some ways, is subsidiary to this larger project in the Saskatchewan river. I say this is subsidiary because the minister has acknowledged it to be so by the issuance of a map. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to it tonight. This map has certain black spots on it showing subsidiary dams all the way up into the Rosthern constituency and my constituency. I did not want to speak in a political tone tonight, but I do want to say in all seriousness and earnestness that I have been more bitterly disappointed tonight than at any time since I came here in 1945.
I had hoped that yesterday the minister merely made a slip of the tongue and, in that persistent way he has, was refusing to acknowledge himself in the wrong. I thought after this debate was over everything would be sweetness and light, and we would be back to where we were before with regard to this whole project. I am now convinced in my mind that the government has abandoned the Saskatchewan project. 1 cannot come to any other conclusion.
It is our child; why should we abandon it?

The minister told me on an occasion when I went out to make a speech, which he has referred to as "that speech", that it would lose me the election in the Hanley territory. It did not. Although I want to be modest, I can say that my majority was trebled over that of the 1945 election. That is not what I came to tell you about, however. The minister was rather annoyed at me when I suggested on several occasions he was pussyfooting about this particular project and making a political football out of it. I have now come to the reluctant conclusion that I was right.
The election was won by the Liberal party, and they made a fine showing in Saskatchewan. May I give the minister all the credit for that, much more credit than I would give the Liberal leader in that particular province.
Supply-Agriculture
There are two things to which I give credit for the Liberal victory. The first is the astuteness of the Minister of Agriculture and the second is the promises which were made in regard to this particular water project. The Minister of Agriculture has returned to this house with what I call his cheering section, the fourteen Liberal members gained at the expense of this party in the province of Saskatchewan. I should like to ask them tonight if they will get up during this debate-

It being eleven o'clock, shall I report progress?
Progress reported.

speechtext: On Monday next we will proceed with the notice of motion concerning an act to amend the British North America Act, which is in the name of the Prime Minister. We will then take up the second reading of Bill No. 12, to establish the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. If we can reach the next item, it will be the second reading of Bill No. 62, an act respecting forest conservation. If those bills are completed, we will move to go into supply, calling two new departments and completing the Agriculture estimates.

May I ask the hon. minister a question? I understood him to say that two new departments will be called if there is a motion to go into supply. About thirteen departments have been put in so far, so there are only three remaining; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. I hesitate to say there are six, but I am sure of five departments that are to come.
I would suggest the government be satisfied with putting in one department on this occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are always ready to accept a suggestion from my hon. friend.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, October 17, 1949
